title: Umami, the fifth basic taste: Ikeda's 1908 discovery in kombu broth and the later discovery of glutamate receptors

sources.title: Umami the Fifth Basic Taste: History of Studies on Receptor Mechanisms and Role as a Food Flavor

facts.text: In 1908 Kikunae Ikeda, a professor of chemistry at the University of Tokyo, identified glutamate as the source of the special taste of kombu seaweed broth (dashi).
The taste Ikeda studied was not sweet, sour, salty or bitter; at the time those four were seen as the basic tastes.
Ikeda extracted glutamate crystals from a large amount (12 kg) of dried kombu and named the taste umami, from a Japanese word for delicious.
About a year after his discovery, Ikeda helped found the company Ajinomoto to make and sell glutamate as a seasoning.
In 1913 Shintaro Kodama, Ikeda's student, found that a different substance, inosinate, gives dried bonito its umami taste.
Japanese dashi is often made with both kombu and dried bonito flakes.
Umami substances taste rather weak on their own; for a long time umami was not accepted in Europe and America, and glutamate was called a flavor enhancer.
Around 2000 to 2002, scientists identified receptors on taste cells that respond to glutamate, which helped establish umami as the fifth basic taste.
Glutamate is the most common amino acid in proteins, so umami is seen as a signal of protein in food.
Human breast milk contains a high level of glutamate, similar to the level in kombu dashi.
Foods rich in umami include seaweed, dried fish, mushrooms, tomatoes, meat and cheese.
